newsitem.title: SRI LANKA: Gas strike threatens to shut Sri Lanka industry.
newsitem.headline: Gas strike threatens to shut Sri Lanka industry.

text.p: Sri Lankan industries which use liquid petroleum gas (LPG) said on Wednesday they may be forced to shut down as a strike at the island's monopoly gas distributor entered its fifth day.
"We are faced with a terrible situation," said Shirley Gurusinghe, general manager of Ceylon Glass Company, which uses about two tonnes of LPG per day.
"Right now we are running at about one-third of capacity. But our production will come to a complete halt when the tanks run out of gas, which should be sometime tonight," Gurusinghe told Reuters.
The company has not estimated its losses if it is forced to shut down.
Talks between trade union leaders, company and government officials to end a strike at Shell Gas Lanka Ltd., owned by the Royal Dutch/Shell Group Shell, failed to produce results on Tuesday.
An official for the Ministry of Labour said talks would resume on Thursday.

The strike was launched last Friday by workers of the All Ceylon Commercial and Industrial Workers Union demanding an immediate halt to transfers of employees and the reinstatement of six workers who were dismissed.
Several industries faced the threat of closing down as their LPG stocks dwindled five days into the strike.

"We have stopped most of our machines and the rest will have to come to a halt most probably tonight," said Harischandra Samarasekera, general manager of Amico Industries, which supplies corks for several soft drink bottlers.
Amico, which also uses about two tonnes of LPG per day, said a shutdown could result in lost production totalling about 2.4 million rupees (US$40,000) per day.
Both Ceylon Glass and Amico said their LPG storage tanks were expected to run dry by Wednesday night or Thursday.
"This monopolistic situation is hurting our industry," said Patrick Amerasinghe, president of the Federation of Chambers of Commerce and Industry.
"Industries can't get gas from another supplier because in Sri Lanka no one else is allowed to sell LPG other than Shell," Amerasinghe said.
Samarasekera said his company had applied for permission from the government to purchase LPG from the Ceylon Petroleum Corporation, but so far has had no response.
Officials for Shell Gas Lanka were not available for comment.
A ship with 1,750 tonnes of gas has been waiting outside Colombo port since Saturday, unable to unload because of the strike.
State radio on Wednesday said domestic LPG consumers were badly affected and many restaurants have been forced to cut down on service with distribution coming to a standstill.
Supplies were being maintained only to hospitals and to essential services like the military, the radio said.
This is the second strike at the company since it was privatised in October 1995.
